title: Kasa Learning Academy

modules.subtitle: Build your foundations
modules.description: Work with values, logic and decisions.

lessons.title: Welcome to Kasa
lessons.subtitle: Write your first ideas in a language you know.
lessons.overview: Kasa is a Twi-first programming language. It uses short words such as ka (print), ma (assign) and sɛ (if) to teach the same computational ideas used in other languages. The language is experimental: its vocabulary is still being reviewed by Twi speakers and educators.
points: Programming is a set of instructions
A program tells a computer what to do. Kasa reads your instructions from top to bottom unless a condition, loop or function changes that order.
The editor on this page runs Kasa locally in your browser. It does not send the code you type to a server.
lessons.code:
# First Kasa program
ka "Maakye, Ghana!"
ka "Meda wo ase!"
lessons.task: Change the second greeting, run the program again and observe the new output.

quiz.question: What does ka do?
quiz.explanation: ka displays a value or the result of an expression.

lessons.title: Install Kasa
lessons.subtitle: Run .kasa programs on your computer.
lessons.overview: You can program instantly in the online editor, but local installation is useful for longer projects, offline development and command-line workflows. The current Python CLI needs Python 3.11 or newer. A separate experimental native C++ compiler exists for developers.
points: You can complete this course entirely in your browser. Select a lesson, edit a program and press Run code.
Install Python 3.11+, Git, and a terminal. The setup guide has Windows, macOS and Linux commands.
Save programs in UTF-8 as hello.kasa, not hello.py. Kasa has its own grammar.
lessons.code:
# Save this as hello.kasa
ka "My Kasa setup works!"
lessons.task: Open the Setup page using the button below the example. Follow your operating system instructions, then run hello.kasa.

quiz.question: Which source file extension is used by Kasa?
quiz.explanation: Kasa programs normally use the .kasa extension.

lessons.title: Hello, Ghana!
lessons.subtitle: Print text, numbers and calculations.
lessons.overview: The first keyword to learn is ka. It prints text inside double quotes, numeric values, or an expression.
points: Double quotes mark text. Numbers are written without quotes. Kasa evaluates a calculation before printing its result.
Programs contain statements on separate lines. A comment starts with # and explains the code to people.
lessons.code:
# Printing in Kasa
ka "Akwaaba!"
ka 4 + 6
ka "Kasa yɛ dɛ"
lessons.task: Change 4 + 6 to 12 * 3 and rerun.

quiz.question: Which statement prints the number 10?
quiz.explanation: Use ka before the value you want displayed.

lessons.title: Variables with ma
lessons.subtitle: Remember information by giving it a name.
lessons.overview: Variables are named values. ma assigns a name to text, numbers, lists, or other values. The name can contain Twi characters such as ɛ and ɔ.
points: The statement ma din = "Ama" creates a variable named din. You can change it later with another ma statement.
Use + to join two text values. To join text and a number, explicitly convert the number with nsɛm().
lessons.code:
ma edin = "Akosua"
ma mfe = 18
ka "Maakye, " + edin
ka "Age: " + nsɛm(mfe)
ma mfe = mfe + 1
ka mfe
lessons.task: Change edin, then increase mfe by 5 instead of 1.

quiz.question: Which keyword assigns a value?
quiz.explanation: ma gives a variable a value.

lessons.title: Data types
lessons.subtitle: Numbers, text, booleans, lists and hwee.
lessons.overview: Kasa distinguishes whole numbers, decimals, text, Boolean values, lists and no-value (hwee). These types matter because not every operation makes sense for every value.
points: nokware means true and atoro means false. Kasa does not silently treat them as 1 and 0.
Use nɔma("12") to convert numeric text to a number, and nsɛm(12) to convert a number to text.
lessons.code:
ka 42
ka 3.5
ka "Ghana"
ka nokware
ka atoro
ka hwee
ka nɔma("12") + 5
lessons.task: Try ka "12" + 5. Read the error, then fix it using nɔma().

quiz.question: Which value represents Boolean true?
quiz.explanation: nokware is Kasa true, atoro is false.

lessons.title: Arithmetic and order
lessons.subtitle: Build reliable calculations.
lessons.overview: Kasa supports +, -, *, / and % (whole-number remainder). Parentheses control evaluation order. Division produces a decimal result.
points: Multiplication is evaluated before addition. Use parentheses to change the order.
For example, text + number is an error. Use nsɛm() or nɔma() intentionally.
lessons.code:
ma a = 7
ma b = 3
ka a + b
ka a * b
ka 2 + 3 * 4
ka (2 + 3) * 4
ka 7 % 3
lessons.task: Change a and b, and predict the output before running.

quiz.question: What is the result of 2 + 3 * 4?
quiz.explanation: Multiplication happens first, so 3 * 4 is 12.

lessons.title: Comparisons and logic
lessons.subtitle: Ask true-or-false questions.
lessons.overview: Conditions use comparison operators such as ==, !=, <, >, <= and >=. Combine Boolean values with ne (and), anaa (or) and ɛnyɛ (not).
points: = assigns inside ma. == checks whether two expressions are equal.
With ne, Kasa skips the right-hand side if the left is false. With anaa, it skips the right side if the left is true.
lessons.code:
ma age = 21
ma has_card = nokware
ka age >= 18
ka age >= 18 ne has_card
ka age < 18 anaa has_card
ka ɛnyɛ has_card
lessons.task: Change age to 16 and has_card to atoro. Predict which results change.

quiz.question: What does ne mean?
quiz.explanation: ne is logical AND. Both sides must be true.

lessons.title: Decisions with sɛ
lessons.subtitle: Make a program choose between actions.
lessons.overview: Use sɛ for if, anyɛ_saa_a for else, and awiei to close the block. The letter a ends the if condition header; omitting it is a syntax error.
points: A condition such as score >= 50 returns nokware or atoro. Kasa does not allow numbers in place of booleans.
You can put another sɛ block inside a branch. Every opened block needs its own awiei.
lessons.code:
ma score = 68
sɛ score >= 80 a
    ka "Grade A"
anyɛ_saa_a
    sɛ score >= 50 a
        ka "Passed"
    anyɛ_saa_a
        ka "Try again"
    awiei
awiei
lessons.task: Change score to 92, then to 42.

quiz.question: Which keyword ends an if block?
quiz.explanation: awiei closes conditional, loop and function blocks.

lessons.title: Repeat with mpɛn
lessons.subtitle: Do something an exact number of times.
lessons.overview: mpɛn repeats a block a non-negative whole number of times. It is useful for fixed repetitions and generating simple patterns.
points: mpɛn 3 executes the body three times.
The execution engine applies limits to protect your browser from runaway programs.
lessons.code:
ma total = 0
mpɛn 5
    ma total = total + 10
    ka "Saving 10"
awiei
ka "Total: " + nsɛm(total)
lessons.expected:
Saving 10
Saving 10
Saving 10
Saving 10
Saving 10
Total: 50
lessons.task: Change the repeat count to 8 and the savings to 15.

quiz.question: How many times does mpɛn 4 execute its block?
quiz.explanation: mpɛn uses a counted repetition.

lessons.title: While loops
lessons.subtitle: Repeat while a condition remains true.
lessons.overview: bere_a means while. It repeats a block as long as its condition evaluates to nokware. Update the variables in the condition to avoid an accidental infinite loop.
points: A counter often starts at 1 and increases each time through the loop.
gyae exits the nearest loop. toa_so skips to the next iteration; be careful to advance counters before continuing.
lessons.code:
ma n = 1
bere_a n <= 5
    ka n * n
    ma n = n + 1
awiei
lessons.task: Change the stop condition from n <= 5 to n <= 8.

quiz.question: What happens when bere_a keeps seeing nokware?
quiz.explanation: A while loop continues while the condition is true, subject to safety limits.

lessons.title: Functions with dwumadie
lessons.subtitle: Reuse logic and return values.
lessons.overview: A function is a reusable block of instructions. Define it with dwumadie, give it parameters, and use sanma to return a value.
points: Parameters receive values from a call. sanma exits a function and provides its result.
Function parameters and local variables do not automatically overwrite the same names outside the function.
lessons.code:
dwumadie mfaso(revenue, cost)
    sanma revenue - cost
awiei

ka mfaso(250, 170)
ka mfaso(900, 400)
lessons.task: Add a third profit calculation and display the result.

quiz.question: What does sanma do?
quiz.explanation: sanma returns a value from a function.

lessons.title: Recursion
lessons.subtitle: A function can call itself.
lessons.overview: Recursive functions solve a problem by calling themselves with a smaller version of that problem. A base case prevents recursion from continuing forever.
points: When n <= 1, the factorial function returns 1 immediately.
Otherwise, multiply n by the factorial of n - 1. Kasa limits recursion depth for safety.
lessons.code:
dwumadie factorial(n)
    sɛ n <= 1 a
        sanma 1
    awiei
    sanma n * factorial(n - 1)
awiei
ka factorial(5)
lessons.task: Try factorial(6) and predict the answer.

quiz.question: Why does a recursive function need a base case?
quiz.explanation: Without a terminating condition recursion would not stop.

lessons.title: Lists and indexes
lessons.subtitle: Store many values under one name.
lessons.overview: A list stores a sequence of values. Access items using zero-based indexes: index 0 means the first element. tentɛn() returns the number of items.
points: If a list has three items, valid indexes are 0, 1 and 2.
Lists can contain numbers, strings and nested lists. Invalid indexes produce an error.
lessons.code:
ma prices = [20, 40, 60]
ka prices[0]
ka prices[2]
ka tentɛn(prices)
ka prices[0] + prices[1]
lessons.task: Add another price and print the new list length.

quiz.question: What index accesses the first list item?
quiz.explanation: Kasa lists are zero-indexed.

lessons.title: Change and analyze lists
lessons.subtitle: Update list elements inside a loop.
lessons.overview: List values are mutable. Use ma list[index] = value to update an element. A while loop can traverse the list and total its values.
points: The operation ma prices[1] = 55 changes the second value.
Keep an index i, loop while it is less than tentɛn(prices), and increment i after processing each item.
lessons.code:
ma amounts = [10, 20, 30]
ma amounts[1] = 25
ma i = 0
ma total = 0
bere_a i < tentɛn(amounts)
    ma total = total + amounts[i]
    ma i = i + 1
awiei
ka amounts[1]
ka total
lessons.task: Change amounts[0] to 100, then calculate the new total.

quiz.question: What does ma amounts[1] = 25 change?
quiz.explanation: Index 1 is the second element.

lessons.title: User input with bisa
lessons.subtitle: Make your programs interactive.
lessons.overview: bisa() reads one line of input and returns text. In the browser, type each answer on its own line in the Program input box before pressing Run.
points: If your program calls bisa() twice, provide two separate lines in the input box.
Use nɔma(bisa()) if you intend to add or multiply the entered value.
lessons.code:
ka "Wo din de sɛn?"
ma edin = bisa()
ka "Akwaaba, " + edin
lessons.expected:
Wo din de sɛn?
Akwaaba, Ama
lessons.task: Replace the Program input text with your own name. Confirm that the greeting changes.

quiz.question: What type does bisa() return?
quiz.explanation: bisa() returns a string, even when you enter digits.

lessons.title: Debug your Kasa code
lessons.subtitle: Read and fix mistakes.
lessons.overview: A syntax error means the grammar is incorrect. A runtime error occurs after valid code starts executing, such as dividing by zero or referring to an unknown variable.
points: Kasa errors include the source line and column so you can find a mistake quickly.
Use Check syntax to validate the program without executing it. Then run it to test its behavior.
lessons.code:
ma a = 15
ma b = 3
ka a / b
lessons.task: Change b to 0, observe the runtime error, then restore a nonzero value.

quiz.question: Does Check syntax execute your program?
quiz.explanation: Syntax checking parses the source without running it.

lessons.title: Savings goal calculator
lessons.subtitle: Model a simple savings plan.
lessons.overview: Use variables, a loop and decisions to calculate how quickly a savings goal can be achieved. This example uses simple whole-number amounts and does not model interest.
points: The current savings grows by monthly savings on each iteration.
The condition current >= goal determines whether to stop.
lessons.code:
ma goal = 1000
ma monthly = 250
ma current = 0
ma months = 0
bere_a current < goal
    ma current = current + monthly
    ma months = months + 1
awiei
ka "Months needed: " + nsɛm(months)
ka "Saved: " + nsɛm(current)
lessons.task: Change goal to 1500 and monthly to 200. Predict the number of months.

quiz.question: Which construct keeps accumulating until a goal is reached?
quiz.explanation: A while loop continues until the goal condition changes.

lessons.title: Student results analyzer
lessons.subtitle: Calculate averages and pass counts.
lessons.overview: Apply the same programming ideas to a set of student marks. The program counts passes, sums scores and calculates the class average.
points: Loop over every mark and update a running total.
A mark of 50 or more counts as a pass in this example. Different schools can change that threshold.
lessons.code:
ma marks = [90, 70, 40, 60]
ma total = 0
ma passed = 0
ma i = 0
bere_a i < tentɛn(marks)
    ma total = total + marks[i]
    sɛ marks[i] >= 50 a
        ma passed = passed + 1
    awiei
    ma i = i + 1
awiei
ka "Average: " + nsɛm(total / tentɛn(marks))
ka "Passed: " + nsɛm(passed)
lessons.task: Add another score to marks and compare the average.

quiz.question: What does tentɛn(marks) return?
quiz.explanation: tentɛn() returns the length of a list.

lessons.title: Mini inventory report
lessons.subtitle: Combine lists, conditions and accounting.
lessons.overview: Build a small product-reporting program using sales, costs and quantities. Compute total sales, cost of goods sold (COGS) and gross profit. The result is for learning; real systems also need persistence and controls.
points: The current Kasa browser language has no database/file/network standard library. These amounts are stored in memory only.
lessons.code:
ma products = ["Battery", "Oil", "Filter"]
ma sold = [3, 10, 5]
ma price = [250, 55, 40]
ma cost = [180, 35, 20]
ma revenue = 0
ma cogs = 0
ma i = 0
bere_a i < tentɛn(products)
    ka products[i]
    ma revenue = revenue + sold[i] * price[i]
    ma cogs = cogs + sold[i] * cost[i]
    ma i = i + 1
awiei
ka "Sales: " + nsɛm(revenue)
ka "COGS: " + nsɛm(cogs)
ka "Profit: " + nsɛm(revenue - cogs)
lessons.expected:
Battery
Oil
Filter
Sales: 1500
COGS: 990
Profit: 510
lessons.task: Add a fourth product to all four lists and recalculate profit.

quiz.question: How is gross profit calculated?
quiz.explanation: Gross profit equals revenue minus cost of goods sold.

lessons.title: Sorting algorithm
lessons.subtitle: Use nested loops to order values.
lessons.overview: A sorting algorithm rearranges items into a chosen order. Bubble sort is not the fastest algorithm, but it is an excellent exercise in comparisons, loops and list mutation.
points: If the left value is larger than the right one, swap them.
The outer loop makes passes. The inner loop compares neighboring positions.
Bubble sort generally takes quadratic time, so it is mainly educational for larger inputs.
lessons.code:
ma values = [9, 2, 7, 1, 5]
ma i = 0
bere_a i < tentɛn(values)
    ma j = 0
    bere_a j < tentɛn(values) - i - 1
        sɛ values[j] > values[j + 1] a
            ma temp = values[j]
            ma values[j] = values[j + 1]
            ma values[j + 1] = temp
        awiei
        ma j = j + 1
    awiei
    ma i = i + 1
awiei
ka values
lessons.task: Change the starting values and confirm the results are in increasing order.

quiz.question: Which operation swaps two list values safely?
choices: Store one in a temporary variable
quiz.explanation: A temporary variable preserves the old value during the swap.

lessons.title: Market-day profit and margin
lessons.subtitle: Understand sales, cost and what a trader keeps.
lessons.overview: A trader can sell many items and still earn little if costs are high. Model sales revenue, purchase costs and profit in Kasa. This is a learning calculation, not a complete business accounting statement.
points: Revenue is the amount earned from sales. Cost is the amount spent to acquire the goods sold; in this simplified example we omit rent, transport and other expenses.
Profit = revenue - cost. Profit margin as a percentage = profit / revenue * 100 when revenue is greater than zero.
Run the program with lower sales or higher costs. A negative profit means the simplified sale lost money.
lessons.code:
ma revenue = 500
ma cost = 350
ma profit = revenue - cost
ma margin = profit / revenue * 100
ka "Profit"
ka profit
ka "Margin percent"
ka margin
lessons.task: Change revenue to 800 and cost to 620. Calculate profit and margin before you run the program.

quiz.question: If revenue is 500 and cost is 350, what is profit?
quiz.explanation: Subtract cost from sales revenue: 500 - 350 = 150.

lessons.title: School results: averages and decisions
lessons.subtitle: Calculate an average mark and check a pass threshold.
lessons.overview: Build a transparent three-subject average for a classroom exercise. This introduces arithmetic, reusable variables and a conditional outcome without needing external data or libraries.
points: Sum the subject marks, then divide by the number of subjects. Here three marks are each on a scale of 0 to 100.
The pass threshold in this exercise is 50. Actual school grading rules may be different.
Test averages of 49, 50 and 51 to see exactly where the decision changes.
lessons.code:
ma maths = 80
ma science = 70
ma english = 60
ma average = (maths + science + english) / 3
ka average
sɛ average >= 50 a
    ka "Pass"
anyɛ_saa_a
    ka "Review"
awiei
lessons.task: Set the marks to 45, 50 and 55. Predict the result, then change the threshold from 50 to 60.

quiz.question: Which expression calculates the average of three marks?
quiz.explanation: Parentheses ensure all three marks are added before division.

lessons.title: Inventory restock alert
lessons.subtitle: Decide when a small shop needs new stock.
lessons.overview: Track units in stock after sales, then print a message when the remaining quantity reaches a reorder point. This is a practical introduction to decisions and basic inventory control.
points: Closing units = opening units - units sold. Real stock records should also include purchases, returns and damaged stock.
The threshold is a policy set by a shopkeeper. At or below 10 units, this exercise recommends restocking.
In a production application, validate sales against stock and record transactions before updating balances.
lessons.code:
ma opening = 40
ma sold = 32
ma remaining = opening - sold
ka "Remaining units"
ka remaining
sɛ remaining <= 10 a
    ka "Restock"
anyɛ_saa_a
    ka "Stock okay"
awiei
lessons.task: Change sold to 20, then 35. When does the warning first appear? Add your own reorder threshold.

quiz.question: When opening stock is 40 and sales are 32, how many remain?
quiz.explanation: Closing units are 40 - 32 = 8.

lessons.title: Plan a savings target
lessons.subtitle: Repeat monthly contributions and track the total.
lessons.overview: A savings goal is easier to understand when you model regular contributions. Use a counted loop to accumulate an amount month by month. Interest and fees are deliberately excluded.
points: The total starts at zero. Each repetition adds one fixed monthly contribution.
After six contributions of 150, the total is 900. The model assumes every contribution is made.
Try different monthly amounts and compare six versus twelve months.
lessons.code:
ma total = 0
mpɛn 6
    ma total = total + 150
awiei
ka "Saved"
ka total
lessons.task: Make the contribution 200 and the duration 12 months. Predict the saved amount and confirm by running.

quiz.question: How much is saved with six contributions of 150 and no interest?
quiz.explanation: Six equal contributions of 150 add to 900.

practices.hint: Use sanma a + b inside a function, then call ka add(7, 8).

practices.task: Given scores = [10, 20, 30], print their average as a decimal.
practices.hint: Add the three indexed values and divide by tentɛn(scores).

practices.task: Count the even numbers in [2, 5, 8, 11, 14] and print the count.
practices.start:
ma values = [2, 5, 8, 11, 14]
ma count = 0
# Complete your loop
practices.hint: An integer is even when value % 2 == 0.

practices.title: A profit check
practices.task: Use revenue = 1500 and cogs = 990; print Profit: 510 using variables and nsɛm().
practices.start:
ma revenue = 1500
ma cogs = 990
# Print profit with a label

practices.title: Market day receipt
practices.task: A trader sells 3 notebooks for 12 Ghana cedis each and 2 pens for 5 each. Print exactly Total GHS: 46 using arithmetic and nsɛm().
practices.start:
ma books = 3
ma book_price = 12
ma pens = 2
ma pen_price = 5
# Compute both item totals, then print a labeled receipt
practices.hint: Compute books * book_price + pens * pen_price, then join the number to "Total GHS: " using nsɛm().

practices.title: School result decision
practices.task: A pupil has marks 65, 70 and 75. Print the average followed by Pass on the next line if the average is at least 50. Use the three values supplied.
practices.start:
ma maths = 65
ma english = 70
ma science = 75
# Compute the average, then use sɛ to test it
practices.hint: Divide the sum by 3, print the average, then use sɛ average >= 50 a ... awiei.

practices.title: Stock reorder control
practices.task: Start with 50 units and record 43 units sold. Print Stock: 7 and then Reorder on the next line when stock is at most 10.
practices.start:
ma opening = 50
ma sold = 43
# Calculate remaining stock and flag low quantities
practices.hint: Calculate opening - sold. Use nsɛm() for the labeled number and sɛ remaining <= 10 a for the warning.

practices.title: Savings club contribution report
practices.task: A savings club deposits 80 Ghana cedis each month for 6 months. Use mpɛn to accumulate contributions and print Saved GHS: 480.
practices.start:
ma total = 0
ma monthly = 80
# Repeat deposits, then print the result
practices.hint: Use mpɛn 6, update total with ma total = total + monthly, close with awiei.

practices.title: Transport fare estimator
practices.task: A trotro journey costs 7 Ghana cedis per passenger. Use a reusable Kasa function to calculate the fare for 5 passengers and print Fare GHS: 35.
practices.start:
# Define dwumadie fare(passengers, price)
# Return the product; use the function to print total
practices.hint: Use dwumadie fare(passengers, price), sanma passengers * price, awiei, and then ka "Fare GHS: " + nsɛm(fare(5, 7)).

glossary: Length of text or a list
